essays.text:
It was a grey Tuesday afternoon. Mia was waiting for her friend outside the library when she noticed that the red bike had vanished. Someone had cut the old lock, and a few metal pieces were lying on the ground.

Mia decided to investigate. First, she questioned the librarian, who had seen a tall boy near the racks earlier. Then she spoke to a gardener who was watering the flowers across the street. He remembered that a delivery van had stopped there for a few minutes, although he had not paid much attention to it.

The clues seemed confusing. However, Mia found a small receipt under a bench. It came from the bike shop on Maple Street, and it was dated that very morning. When she arrived at the shop, the owner was repairing a red bike with a broken chain.

In the end, the mystery was simple. The owner's son had borrowed the bike because his own had broken, and he had forgotten to tell his sister. Everybody laughed, and the bike went back to the library before closing time.

Last winter, a tiny detail changed my whole year. I had set my alarm for seven o'clock, but my phone had died during the night, so I woke up late and missed the school bus by thirty seconds.

Because of that, I walked to school through the park, and I met an old man who was feeding the birds. He told me that he had been a music teacher for forty years, and he offered to give me free guitar lessons. Today, I play in a small band with my friends.

If I hadn't missed the bus, I would have arrived on time, and I would have walked past him without a word. I would have spent my evenings in front of the television, and I wouldn't have discovered how much I love music. Honestly, my life would have been far more boring.

Sometimes I wish I had thanked him properly before he moved away last spring. If only I had asked for his address! Still, I feel relieved and grateful, because that annoying morning turned out to be the luckiest day of my life.

Dear Selection Committee,

I am writing to apply for a place in your international exchange programme in Montreal next year. I am a sixteen-year-old student from Lyon, and I have been studying English and Spanish for several years. Furthermore, I volunteer every Saturday at a local food bank, where I assist elderly visitors and help to organise donations.

What attracts me most to this programme is the opportunity to live with a host family and to experience daily life in a bilingual city. I firmly believe that a language is learned through real conversations rather than through textbooks alone. Moreover, studying abroad would allow me to become more independent and open-minded.

In return, I would bring curiosity, reliability and a genuine desire to contribute to my host school. It was my experience at the food bank that taught me how to listen carefully, work in a team and remain calm under pressure. Therefore, I am confident that I could adapt quickly to a new environment.

I would be grateful if you could inform me of the next steps of the selection process. I have attached my school reports and a reference letter from my English teacher, and I would be happy to attend an interview at your convenience.

Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,

Sam Martin

Last Friday, I attended the opening night of Cirque Aurora, a new show that promises to blend acrobatics with storytelling. On the whole, it delivers an enchanting evening, although a few scenes drag on far too long.

The first act is undoubtedly the strongest. A clown strides onto the stage, glances nervously at the audience and mutters an apology, as if he had wandered into the wrong theatre. Within seconds, the children around me were giggling, and even the most serious adults chuckled. Moreover, the trapeze artists fly so gracefully that they look as though gravity has simply forgotten them.

However, the second half is less convincing. The storyline becomes confusing, and a long dance number seems to exist only to give the technicians time to change the set. In addition, one juggler stumbles twice, which breaks the magic, even though the crowd whispered words of encouragement. Consequently, the energy drops just when it should be rising towards the finale.

Nevertheless, the closing scene, in which forty performers build a human tower beneath a shower of golden light, is truly breathtaking. Overall, despite its uneven pacing, Cirque Aurora is a generous and inventive show. I would recommend it to families and to anyone who needs to rediscover a sense of wonder, but I would advise them to book seats near the front, where every detail can be appreciated.

Dear Editor,

I was dismayed to read in last week's edition that the town council intends to close the central public library and replace it with a so-called digital hub. While I appreciate that budgets are under considerable pressure, I believe this proposal fundamentally misunderstands what the library represents for our community.

For many residents, the library is far more than a collection of books. It is one of the few remaining places where anyone, regardless of income or age, can spend an afternoon without being expected to buy anything. Pensioners read the newspapers there, students who lack a quiet room at home revise for their examinations, and parents attend the weekly storytelling sessions with their toddlers. Furthermore, the librarians provide invaluable guidance to people who struggle with online forms, a service that no automated terminal could ever replace.

Admittedly, the building is expensive to heat and maintain, and visitor numbers have declined slightly over the past decade. Consequently, some reorganisation may well be necessary. However, closing the library altogether would be a short-sighted decision whose social costs would far outweigh the modest savings.

Instead, I would urge the council to consider more imaginative alternatives. The ground floor could be shared with a café or a community association, thereby generating rental income. Moreover, local businesses might be invited to sponsor specific programmes, such as coding clubs or language exchanges, which would attract younger users. Finally, opening hours could be adjusted to match actual demand rather than being cut indiscriminately.

Had the council consulted residents before announcing its plan, it would have discovered how deeply attached people are to this institution. I sincerely hope that it will reconsider before an irreplaceable public space is lost forever.

Yours faithfully,

Daniel Moreau
